title: This Photo of the ISS Next to Jupiter Was Two Years in the Making - Nautilus
gist: Profile of astrophotographer AJ Smadi's two-year-planned image of the ISS passing in front of Jupiter, part of his 'ISS Meets' series. It covers his planning method, his equipment (9.25-inch Celestron SCT, ZWO ASI662MC) and the sub-second capture window.

insights.claim: AJ Smadi planned a photograph of the International Space Station passing in front of Jupiter for about two years, checking the ISS path against the gas giant's movements roughly every month.
insights.speaker: AJ Smadi
insights.so_what: Shows how much planning hobbyist astrophotography takes and how dedicated its users are, which supports demand for niche optics.
insights.quote: Every month or so for the past couple years, I would check the ISS’s path across the sky

insights.claim: Jupiter is about 1.3 million times bigger than the ISS but also about 1.3 million times farther away, so the two appear at a similar scale in the photo.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Explains why the alignment works visually.
insights.quote: Jupiter is about 1.3 million times bigger than the ISS, but it’s also around 1.3 million times further away

insights.claim: Smadi drove over an hour north of Seattle to Burlington, Washington, before sunrise to capture the alignment, because the shot depends on being at a precise location on Earth.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Alignment shots depend on location, which drives travel and planning tools for amateur astronomers.

insights.claim: The shot is part of Smadi's 'ISS Meets' series, which has included Venus and Saturn, with 'ISS Meets Mercury' planned next.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: A serial creator project of this kind shows how far citizen astrophotography has advanced.

insights.claim: Seven ISS residents were aboard at the time of the photo: Jessica Watkins, Luke Delaney, Joshua Kutryk, Sergey Teteryatnikov, Pyotr Dubrov, Anil Menon and Anna Kikina; a wider frame also captured Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.

insights.claim: The equipment was a 9.25-inch Celestron Schmidt-Cassegrain telescope with a 2,350 mm focal length and a ZWO ASI662MC camera with a Sony IMX662 sensor, plus UV and IR blocking filters.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Consumer astronomy hardware from Celestron, ZWO and Sony now enables results close to professional quality.

insights.claim: Top astrophotography requires calculating when objects will pass each other, working out the exact viewing location on Earth, and capturing the event in a window much shorter than a second.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Prediction and orbit-tracking software is a key enabler for this hobby.
insights.quote: capturing a photo of the event within a window significantly shorter than a second
